conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time for this today. I’m Dr. Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you settle into life with your new baby.

To do that, I’m going to walk through a short questionnaire called the EPDS. It’s a 10-item screen that looks at how you’ve been coping emotionally over the past seven days. It’s not a test of your parenting—just a snapshot of how you’re feeling so we can make sure you’re getting the right care. Everything you share here stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger.

We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. When you’re ready, we’ll start.

Over the past week, have you found yourself able to laugh and see the funny side of things as much as usual, or has that felt harder lately?

[pauses, eyes a little glassy]  
Harder lately… I mean, sometimes my husband will make a joke or turn on a sitcom, and I try to smile for his sake, but the laughter just kind of dies in my chest. Things that used to feel funny feel flat now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really... I can force a little chuckle if someone’s watching, but genuine laughter hasn’t happened much this week.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but lately nothing feels worth the effort. Even when I plan something, I’m too tired or worried about the baby to enjoy it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[sighs, eyes dropping to her lap]  
Yeah… I do that a lot. Yesterday the baby was fussy for two straight hours, and I kept thinking it must be something I ate or that I’m not soothing him right. I tell myself I should know what he needs by now—he’s my baby—and if I can’t calm him down, I’m failing him somehow. The guilt just sits in my stomach even after my partner says it’s normal.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

All the time, really. I'll be rocking the baby and suddenly my heart starts racing—what if he stops breathing? What if I trip on the stairs? I check the monitor every few minutes even when he's quiet. My head knows it's probably fine, but I can't shake the worry.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes—especially at night—my chest gets tight and I feel this rush of fear out of nowhere. There’s no real reason; the baby’s asleep, the house is quiet, but it’s like my body is sounding an alarm I can’t turn off. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. Dishes pile up, laundry sits, and I keep thinking, “How does anyone do this?” Sometimes I just stare at the mess and feel frozen, like I don’t even know where to start. I manage the basics—feeding the baby, changing him—but everything else feels too heavy.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[sighs and rubs her forehead]

That’s been happening a lot. When I finally lie down, my mind just keeps running—thinking about everything I didn’t do, worrying the baby might wake up, replaying every little mistake. I’ll toss and turn for an hour or two, then jolt awake at every creak in the house. Even when the baby sleeps a four-hour stretch, I can’t seem to stay asleep the whole time.
I have felt sad or miserable

[slow nod, voice low]  
Most of the day, every day. It’s like a gray cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears just start leaking out, or I’ll catch myself staring at the wall feeling empty. I keep waiting for a “better” moment, but it keeps settling back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods slowly, eyes rimmed red]  
Yeah… I’ve cried three times this week, maybe four. Sometimes it’s because the baby won’t settle and I feel useless; sometimes it just hits me out of nowhere and I end up sobbing over the sink while I wash bottles. I try to keep quiet so my husband doesn’t worry, but the tears just come.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never. I could never leave my baby or my family like that. Some nights I feel so low I think they’d be better off without me, but I’d never act on it. I just want the sadness to stop, not my life.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) interview

Symptoms & Observations  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, frequent tearfulness  
- Marked loss of enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities  
- Excessive guilt/blaming self for infant’s distress  
- Chronic, intrusive worries about infant safety; nocturnal panic episodes  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia related to rumination and hypervigilance  
- Daily sense of being overwhelmed; reduced motivation for household tasks  
- Denies active self-harm ideation or intent; passive “they’d be better off” cognitions noted

Pattern  
Consistent with moderate-to-severe depressive and anxiety symptoms emerging postpartum; functional impairment evident.

Screening Significance  
Elevated probability of Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset and comorbid anxiety; warrants formal diagnostic assessment and safety plan.

Risk Factors Flagged  
– Depressed mood most of the day, crying spells  
– Loss of interest/pleasure  
– Guilt/worthlessness themes  
– Anxiety/panic without clear precipitant  
– Sleep disruption secondary to mood  
– Passive suicidal cognitions (no plan or intent)

Safety  
Denies suicidal intent; no self-harm behaviors reported. Continue to monitor for escalation.

Next Step  
Recommend expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialist for diagnostic clarification and treatment planning.
